bodyText:
Classes and Objects

A class is a blueprint or template that defines the attributes (data) and methods (functions) of a type of object. An object is an instance of a class: a concrete thing created from the blueprint. For example, Car can be a class, while an individual red car with a specific number plate is an object of that class. Many objects can be created from a single class, each with its own attribute values.

Constructors

A constructor is a special method that runs automatically when an object is created. It has the same name as the class and has no return type, not even void. Its job is to initialize the object's data. A default constructor takes no arguments, a parameterized constructor takes arguments, and a copy constructor creates a new object from an existing object of the same class.

Destructors

A destructor is a special method that runs automatically when an object is destroyed or goes out of scope. It releases resources such as memory or open files. In C++, the destructor has the same name as the class prefixed with a tilde, for example ~Car, and it takes no arguments and has no return type. A class has only one destructor, while it may have several constructors.

bodyText:
What is Inheritance?

Inheritance is the mechanism by which a new class acquires the properties and methods of an existing class. The existing class is called the base class (or parent or superclass), and the new class is called the derived class (or child or subclass). Inheritance expresses an 'is-a' relationship: a Student is a Person. Its main benefit is code reusability, since common features are written once in the base class and reused by all derived classes.

Types of Inheritance

  • Single inheritance: one derived class inherits from one base class.
  • Multiple inheritance: one derived class inherits from two or more base classes.
  • Multilevel inheritance: classes form a chain, for example A is the base of B, and B is the base of C.
  • Hierarchical inheritance: several derived classes inherit from a single base class.
  • Hybrid inheritance: a combination of two or more of the above types.

Points to Remember

C++ supports multiple inheritance, while Java does not support it for classes and uses interfaces instead. Multiple inheritance can cause the diamond problem: when a class inherits the same feature through two different paths, it becomes ambiguous which copy to use. Access specifiers control inherited access: public members stay public, protected members are accessible in the class and its derived classes, and private members are accessible only within their own class.

bodyText:
What is Polymorphism?

Polymorphism comes from the Greek words poly (many) and morph (forms): it means one interface taking many forms. The same method name can behave differently depending on the object or the arguments involved. Polymorphism is one of the four pillars of object-oriented programming, along with encapsulation, abstraction and inheritance.

Compile-Time Polymorphism

Compile-time polymorphism, also called static or early binding, is resolved by the compiler before the program runs. Function overloading is its main form: several functions share the same name but differ in the number or types of their parameters, and the compiler chooses the right one. Operator overloading is similar: an operator such as + is given a new meaning for user-defined types.

Runtime Polymorphism

Runtime polymorphism, also called dynamic or late binding, is resolved while the program runs. Its main form is function overriding: a derived class redefines a method of its base class with the same name and signature, and the version that executes depends on the actual object type. In C++, this requires virtual functions. A class containing at least one pure virtual function is an abstract class, and an abstract class cannot be instantiated.

bodyText:
Encapsulation

Encapsulation is the bundling of data and the methods that work on that data into a single unit, the class, while restricting direct access to the data. This restriction is called data hiding. Access specifiers control it: public members are accessible from anywhere, private members are accessible only within the class itself, and protected members are accessible within the class and its derived classes. Controlled access is usually provided through getter and setter methods, so the class can validate changes to its data.

Abstraction

Abstraction means showing only the essential features of an object and hiding the implementation details. A driver uses a car's steering wheel and pedals without knowing how the engine works; similarly, a programmer calls a method without knowing its internal code. Abstraction is achieved through abstract classes and interfaces: an abstract class may contain both implemented and unimplemented methods, while an interface in Java contains only method declarations that implementing classes must define.

Encapsulation vs Abstraction

The two ideas are related but different. Encapsulation is about protecting data: it answers how access is controlled. Abstraction is about simplifying the view: it answers what the user sees. Encapsulation is achieved with access specifiers, while abstraction is achieved with abstract classes and interfaces.

bodyText:
What are Design Patterns?

A design pattern is a proven, reusable solution to a commonly occurring problem in software design. Patterns are not finished code: they are templates that describe how to solve a problem in a way that can be adapted to many situations. The most famous catalogue is the book 'Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software', published in 1994 by Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson and John Vlissides, known as the Gang of Four (GoF). It describes 23 patterns grouped into three categories: creational patterns, which deal with object creation; structural patterns, which deal with the composition of classes and objects; and behavioral patterns, which deal with communication between objects.

Three Essential Patterns

  • Singleton (creational): ensures a class has only one instance and provides a global point of access to it. It is implemented with a private constructor and a static method that returns the single instance. Typical uses are logging, configuration settings and database connections.
  • Factory (creational): the Factory Method pattern defines an interface for creating objects but lets subclasses decide which class to instantiate. Client code asks the factory for an object without knowing the exact class, which keeps object creation logic in one place.
  • Observer (behavioral): defines a one-to-many dependency between objects: when one object (the subject) changes state, all its dependents (observers) are notified automatically. It is the pattern behind event handling in graphical interfaces and the publish-subscribe model.

Other well-known patterns include Adapter and Decorator (structural) and Strategy (behavioral), which lets an algorithm be selected at run time.
